title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
abstract: When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator. This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An ml.p4d.24xlarge has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach. Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation. This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did. One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components , the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned. What customers do today, and why each option falls short If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices. Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not. Use multi-model endpoints – These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic. But models share the device without isolation, so a heavy request for one model affects the others. A model that isn’t loaded also pays a load penalty on first use. Move to self-managed Kubernetes – This is where customers who need real GPU partitioning have gone. MIG works there, but you take on driver versioning, partition configuration, a device plugin, scheduling, and keeping it all consistent across a fleet. That’s a lot of work for a hardware capability your instances already have. Why MIG NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give: Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99. Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU. Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device. No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction. Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler. title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick
abstract: Over the past year, as we built Amazon Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user. Take the user who says “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice. This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When? , What? , Who? , and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it. The framework at a glance Figure 1: How triggers, agents, and capabilities relate, with learning feeding back from the session runtime A trigger starts the work and carries the task ( When and What ), an agent takes it on ( Who ) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task ( How ). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more. Triggers: What causes work to begin Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task. Human-initiated: A person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something. Interactive, synchronous, conversational. Agent-delegated: One agent, mid-task, invokes another to handle a sub-problem. Programmatic, composable, potentially recursive. Scheduled: Time-based activation, like “run financial research every Monday at 9am.” Deterministic, with the same standing instructions applied across runs. Event-driven: A signal from an external system, such as a new email, a Slack mention, a file change, or a webhook. The type of trigger conditions the execution: a scheduled background task might stay conservative (for example, do nothing if uncertain), while a human-initiated one would be responsive (for example, ask rather than stop). Agents We define an agent as a persistent, learning actor . It’s the Who? in any execution, and the anchor against which learning accrues. Two agents given identical input can differ, because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories. The agent isn’t the instructions it follows. It’s the entity that interprets them. It consists of three things: Instructions: Standing guidance defining persona, role, context files, and operating principles. A Finance Agent behaves differently from a general assistant primarily because of this. Capabilities: The tools, skills, workflows, and sub-agents available for use, updated dynamically. A charting library can be added in one session and removed the next. Learned context: Memory that accumulates through use: the queries that work for a tool, the formatting users prefer, the edge cases they care about. This is how the tenth execution beats the first without anyone changing the instructions. Everything else is extrinsic: the large language model (LLM) underlying the agent is a swappable model parameter, conversation history is per-session state, and triggers belong to the platform. title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
abstract: Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort. Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync. In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment. Problem statement and design goals Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model. Integration challenge at scale Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table. Design goals We established four requirements: Configuration-driven data lake access. Adding a dataset requires only a metadata file, not code. Agent-agnostic tool interfaces. Any MCP-compatible client can invoke the same tools. Centralized permission enforcement. Access control is enforced at the MCP server layer. Elastic infrastructure. The system scales with bursty AI workload patterns. Solution overview The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge-base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable. A metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, storing schema descriptions, column-level semantics, and table relationships that the AI agent references when generating SQL. Because the agent derives schema knowledge from the catalog at query time, there is no need to hardcode table structures or redeploy when schemas change. The knowledge-base refresh layer keeps that catalog current, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives. The following sections describe each layer in detail. Architecture walkthrough The following diagram shows the request flow from user query to data layer across all four layers. A user submits a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53 for DNS and reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet, configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer routes to Amazon Cognito, which authenticates the user and enriches the request. Authenticated traffic then enters the private subnet, where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate. This layer handles session state in Amazo

title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
abstract: In Part 1 , you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server. The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools: What Part 1 does Why it stops scaling What Part 2 does instead The agent holds each MCP server’s runtime ARN and calls it directly N agents against M servers is a wiring matrix, and every new tool touches every agent that needs it Agents reach one Gateway endpoint, and the Gateway holds the target registry The agent’s role holds the token-exchange permission and reads the provider’s secret Every agent that acts for users gets a credential path to every resource it might reach The Gateway redeems the grant, and the agent’s role holds no token-exchange or secret permissions Each MCP server carries the same groups check in its own code The same rule, copied into thousands of servers, drifts and can’t be audited or changed in one place One default-deny Cedar policy set, evaluated at the Gateway before tools run In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant. What changes from Part 1 The Okta configuration, the AgentCore Identity credential provider, and the MCP servers from Part 1 stay as they are. Figure 1 shows the architecture with the additions. Figure 1: The Part 1 solution with AgentCore Gateway, Policy, and Observability, a second agent on Amazon EKS, and the audit path, with numbers matching the steps that follow The user signs in, and the backend for frontend (BFF) exchanges the ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) issued to the task agent, agent A, as in Part 1. The BFF invokes agent A on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG. Agent A forwards the ID-JAG to its Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer accepts only agent A’s ID-JAGs. Policy in AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies for each tool listing and each tool call, before the Gateway invokes a target. For calls that Cedar permits, the Gateway has AgentCore Identity redeem the ID-JAG for each target at Okta’s custom authorization server through the Part 1 credential provider. A call that Cedar denies doesn’t redeem the ID-JAG. The MCP server checks the user’s groups and scope, as in Part 1, and records each decision as an authz.check span. Every hop emits OpenTelemetry spans to AgentCore Observability, which CloudWatch Transaction Search collects, and Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge. title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
abstract: An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end. In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. Solution overview Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime. Figure 1: Solution architecture, with numbers matching the steps that follow Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this: The user signs in to the web front end, a backend for frontend (BFF), with OpenID Connect through the agent’s linked Okta app. For each request, the BFF exchanges the user’s ID token for an ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server, authenticated as the agent (RFC 8693 token exchange). Okta checks that the agent is active, that the user is assigned to it, and that an administrator connected it to the target authorization server for the requested scopes. The ID-JAG is single-use and expires in 5 minutes. The BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG as its bearer token. The runtime’s JWT authorizer accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Greenlight Financial resolves more than 90 percent of up to 4,000 security and risk cases each month without human intervention. Greenlight’s Luna uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , infrastructure for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale. Specifically, Greenlight uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to host Luna’s agent code. It uses AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to support its tiered multi-agent system. This avoids the need to build and operate these capabilities in-house. Luna triages dark web breach-card alerts, identity anomalies, and financial-risk events in seconds. This post explains how Greenlight Financial built an autonomous security operations center (SOC) solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover its multi-tiered supervisor architecture, more than 30 specialized agents, episodic memory for continuous learning, and expansion from SOC use cases into financial risk triage. We share production metrics, infrastructure decisions, and patterns for building autonomous security operations in regulated industries. What Greenlight needed to solve Greenlight Financial provides financial products for families: debit cards, savings tools, and connected devices such as the Family Hub and Pet Tracker. The company processes sensitive financial data at scale under the same regulatory requirements as major banks. Greenlight’s SOC receives 3,000–4,000 security and risk alerts per month from four primary vectors: Dark web breach cards – Card Network and internal threat intel flag Greenlight customer cards found on the dark web. Identity and access anomalies – Unusual login patterns, privilege escalations, and policy violations across Identity Provider (IdP) and internal systems. Infrastructure alerts – Signals from Signals from EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), Asset Inventory, and other observability tools. Financial risk events – Suspicious transaction patterns, compliance triggers, and fraud indicators from card processing systems. Each alert demands cross-referencing multiple data sources before an analyst can render a verdict. A single dark web breach card notification requires checking whether the card is active, deduplicating against prior notifications, reviewing customer session data, and checking open support tickets. This workflow takes a human analyst 15-30 minutes per case. At 4,000 cases per month, that math breaks. Greenlight needed a system that could: Triage and resolve routine cases autonomously at machine speed. Escalate complex cases with full context to human analysts. Learn from resolution patterns to improve accuracy over time. Operate within financial services compliance guardrails. Architecture: Tiered multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Greenlight built Luna as a hierarchical multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture follows a tiered supervisor pattern that mirrors how human SOC teams operate. L1 handles volume, and L2 handles complexity. title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Taxbit is a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform. Founded in 2018, Taxbit helps enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers calculate gains and losses, collect tax documentation, and file information returns at scale. Now, a cited, permission-aware AI assistant helps compliance teams find answers right inside the product dashboard. But the knowledge needed to use that dashboard well was scattered across the public website, API documentation, and help-center articles, and a meaningful share was never written down at all. When a customer asked “what does this form status mean?”, they either went digging or filed a support ticket. Today more than 55 percent of users who ask Assist a question return to ask another within 24 hours, according to Taxbit’s internal production analytics. In this post, we share how we built Taxbit Assist , the AI assistant now embedded in the Taxbit dashboard, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. We cover the architecture, the retrieval work that made answers trustworthy enough to ship to regulated customers, how we handle safety and data residency, and how we continuously measure answer quality on live production traffic. What the assistant had to get right A generic chatbot was not an option in this domain. Four constraints shaped what we built: Grounded and cited – Our users make filing decisions. Every answer had to trace back to a source the user could open and read, and when the assistant didn’t know something, it had to say so. Role and organization awareness – The assistant shouldn’t walk a Support User through an admin-only workflow and send them to a page that they can’t open. No tax advice – Explaining how Taxbit computes cost basis (the accounting method used to compute a gain or loss) is product documentation. Telling a user which method to elect is tax advice. The line between the two is narrow. Regional data residency – Supported from a single codebase, with continuous quality measurement in production. Inside our compliance program – Taxbit Assist is developed and operated in line with ISO/IEC 42001, the international standard for AI management systems. Taxbit is also certified to ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27701 and holds a SOC 2 Type II report. Taxbit doesn’t train or fine-tune any model, and Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use prompts or completions to train models. We are also a small team. Rather than build and operate the agent loop, conversation-state store, and session isolation ourselves, we chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for three reasons: its managed agent runtime removed infrastructure operations, built-in AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, eliminated a separate conversation-state store, and per-session isolation kept each user’s context contained. That let us put most of our effort into the retrieval and safety work that follows. title: Extend Claude Code to remote sessions on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with security controls
abstract: You might already run Claude Code locally on your laptop, backed by Amazon Bedrock. This post shows how to go a step further: run it as a remote agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The sample uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so every task runs in its own isolated session inside your AWS account. You offload a coding task, close the laptop, and come back to the result. We first discuss why teams choose Amazon Bedrock for Claude Code and highlight a few key security characteristics. Then, we discuss the remote agent architecture and walk through an accompanying sample, sample-remote-coding-agent , that implements it. The sample runs each task in its own AgentCore runtime session and returns a GitHub pull request for you to review and merge. Along the way, we show how the Amazon Bedrock data controls stay intact when a task runs remotely. Why customers run Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock Customers choose Amazon Bedrock as Claude Code’s model provider for many reasons. These include billing and credits through their existing AWS account with no per-seat licenses, audit logging in AWS CloudTrail, and geographic inference profiles for data residency. Amazon Bedrock also provides three valuable security characteristics: Data protection. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use your content to train models or share it with model providers, and providers can’t access your prompts, completions, or the Amazon Bedrock service logs. Amazon Bedrock is in scope for SOC, ISO, and FedRAMP Moderate, is HIPAA eligible, and can be used in compliance with the GDPR. See Compliance validation for Amazon Bedrock for details. Access through controls you already govern. Claude Code calls Amazon Bedrock with temporary AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials, and you can sign in through an identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta by following the Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock . AWS PrivateLink gives your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) a private connection to Amazon Bedrock. Control over retention and operator access. Mantle, the next-generation inference engine for Amazon Bedrock, is designed for zero operator access (ZOA), so AWS operators have no technical means to access customer data such as your prompts or completions. You also control whether the prompts and outputs from your inference requests are retained. You can configure zero data retention (ZDR) to make sure that no request or response data is written to durable storage by AWS or shared with the model provider. See Data retention and Exploring the zero operator access design of Mantle for details. Why teams add a remote coding agent Remote coding agents have become a common pattern because they turn a coding task into a hand-off. You assign the task, close the laptop or move on to other work, and come back to the result. Several tasks can run at once instead of competing for one machine, and each task runs in its own disposable environment, outside of your laptop and the credentials in your shell. The result comes back as a pull request that a teammate can review like any other change. The pattern has trade-offs: you steer less while a task runs, the environment needs some setup, and cost is harder to predict. The solution in this post runs the work in your own AWS account. Every task runs as an AgentCore runtime session that belongs to your account, and every model call goes to Amazon Bedrock, so those calls inherit the security characteristics described in the previous section. The sample suits some tasks better than others: Good fit. Scoped features, bug fixes, and tests on a trusted repository that declares its own setup and test commands. Not a fit. title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
This Week in AI: The Cost of Progress
abstract: New frontier models arrived this week as investors showed signs of growing cautious about AI spending. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined those developments, along with research into how models learn and the less visible costs of AI adoption. From unequal pricing across languages to the environmental impact of data centers, the discussion raised questions about who benefits from AI progress and who pays for it. Frontier models advance as investors question the spending We started with three model announcements that show how quickly AI capabilities are expanding. Google introduced Gemini 4 Carbon , designed for cybersecurity and complex, multistep tasks. France’s Mistral published the weights for its trillion-parameter Large 4 model , also known as “Le Chonk,” giving developers more control over deployment and customization, provided they have the hardware to run it. Meanwhile, Google DeepMind previewed Genie 4 , a world model that simulates environments, physical interactions, and sequences of events. Unlike language models that predict text, world models attempt to predict what happens when objects and people interact. With Genie 4, researchers could train AI systems in simulated worlds, an approach that would be especially useful in robotics, where teams could test AI designed to control robots before trying it on physical machines. Investor enthusiasm for AI appeared to weaken even as model development accelerated. Anthropic moved closer to a public offering by filing its IPO paperwork publicly , although it hasn’t announced a date or share price. OpenAI has reportedly secured about $11 billion in funding for its latest round, well below its initial $30 billion target. Those developments coincided with sharp declines in several major technology stocks , and the tech-heavy Nasdaq ended October with its worst monthly decline since March 2025. The scale of AI spending is attracting greater scrutiny, particularly as investors wait for returns. Companies investing in AI should pay attention to more than model performance. The economics of training and running increasingly expensive models could affect pricing, availability, and which providers remain competitive. Researchers are rethinking how AI models learn Researchers are investigating how AI models process information, retain knowledge, and generate responses. AI interpretability company Goodfire proposed a project modeled on the Human Genome Project , committing $10 million to begin mapping how large language models work internally. By studying which patterns activate in response to prompts and how changes to those patterns affect behavior, researchers hope to better understand why models produce particular outputs. Google Research proposed a framework inspired by human cognition that introduces a “sleep” phase. During this offline period, models would consolidate new information and generate practice examples through a process researchers call “dreaming.” The goal is to address catastrophic forgetting, when learning new information degrades previously acquired capabilities, while helping models retain knowledge beyond individual conversations. The approach remains experimental, but it offers a possible way for models to continue learning without sacrificing existing skills. We also examined Clover, a 35-billion-parameter diffusion language model released by China’s DiffuSpace. Most familiar language models use what’s called an autoregressive approach: They generate text sequentially, one token at a time. title: Choose Your Coding Harness by What You Need to Control—Not by Who Built It
abstract: Remember back in 2019, when you had only a handful of language models to choose from, all with limited context windows? That world is gone, and it feels like a forgotten past. Today, flagship providers and open source projects compete across model families, sizes, capabilities, and deployment options. Coding harnesses seem to be heading in the same direction. On the surface, Claude Code, Codex, Pi, DeepSeek Harness, and the other coding harnesses all seem to do the same thing: help you build software with models. Look closer, though, and each one gives you control over different parts of the harness. What can the model see and change? How does it use tools? Where does it run, and what happens when it fails? So instead of asking which coding harness is best overall, ask: Which layers of the harness do you need to control? Thanks for all the harnesses! Now what? Choosing a coding harness isn’t only about which model writes the best code. You’re also choosing what the harness provides, what you can change, and what you must build yourself. If it doesn’t give you verification, durable state, repair routing, or an enforced execution boundary, those responsibilities stay with you. You remain accountable for the workflow’s reliability and governance. In general, each harness has a center of gravity: a layer that gives you the most direct control. The following table is a deliberately high-level overview of where that center sits. It’s not a feature matrix, and the boundaries overlap in practice. Claude Code can also run noninteractively and inside sandboxes, Codex also reads repository instructions, and all of them are changing quickly. The point is to show where each harness gives you leverage by default, and where the engineering work is likely to stay with you. Table 1. Where each coding harness puts its primary control Harness Primary control You shape You likely build Claude Code Inside the run Instructions, skills, subagents, hooks Outer lifecycle policy Codex Around execution Sandbox, approvals, scope, output Cross-run orchestration Pi The loop itself Tools, context, state, hand-offs Most defaults DeepSeek Across plug-ins Composable runtime components Gaps in your plug-in set Read the table as a map, not a ranking. A harness that hands you more control also hands you more to build, and a harness that does more out of the box decides more on your behalf. Which trade-off is right depends on which layer your project actually needs to own. Claude Code: Control inside the run Claude Code buys you detailed control over how implementation unfolds. CLAUDE.md provides standing instructions, skills add task-specific playbooks, subagents divide the work, and hooks intercept actions before and after tool calls. Unlike a permission rule that simply refuses an operation, a hook can explain the refusal or immediately return a compiler or policy failure to the agent. These controls let you steer the coding loop extensively, but they operate within Claude Code’s existing lifecycle. If you need to control the outer lifecycle itself, you need another layer. Codex: Control through separation Codex buys you separation between a coding task and its execution environment. A noninteractive codex exec run can work on a narrow task in a specified repository, under an OS-enforced sandbox, and return a schema-constrained result. This is useful for independent verification. You can give Codex a clean checkout, exclude the builder’s instructions, restrict writable paths, and run separate reviews for code quality, test gaps, persistence, or user-visible behavior. The sandbox depends on the operating system, but it moves scope enforcement out of the prompt and into the execution boundary. title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
abstract: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round. Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself. But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors. With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there. But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide. The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing. title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
abstract: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said. title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
abstract: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters. At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors. Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads. Read full article Comments

title: Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now
abstract: A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull. Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5) , indicating a "moderate" brain injury, just one point above "mild." He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5). In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head. title: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
abstract: In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. "This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.” In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth's mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet's interior. Ice and sea The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family." The baby's death is the third measles fatality nationally just this week, following the death of a New York child reported on Monday and another death in Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday . The Pennsylvania death was of an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County; the state health department did not provide additional details, such as the age of the person. title: Could potential AI clones of GTA VI force a quicker official port?
abstract: Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC's DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU , we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator. Obbe Vermeij hasn't worked at Rockstar since 2009 , but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun , he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game's 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release. "So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console," Vermeij said. title: No more Cybertrucks; Musk moves on from the angular metallic flop
abstract: Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs , most likely. Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019 , back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup's unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all. The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y. title: 2026년과 이후 JavaScript의 동향 - 라이브러리와 프레임워크
abstract: "어느 한 프레임워크가 독보적인 위치를 차지하지 않는 상태는 많은 이들에게 희망과 고통을 동시에 안겨준다." 2020년 글 은 이 문장으로 시작했습니다. 6년이 지난 지금, 이 문장은 절반만 맞습니다. 사용률로 보면 React는 독보적인 위치를 굳혔고, 고민은 '어떤 프레임워크를 고를까'에서 'React 위에서 어떤 메타 프레임워크와 빌드 도구를 고를까', 그리고 'AI 도구가 기본값으로 고르는 스택을 그대로 받아들일까'로 옮겨 갔습니다. 여기서 메타 프레임워크는 UI 라이브러리 위에 라우팅, 서버 렌더링(SSR), 빌드 구성을 더한 프레임워크(Next.js, Nuxt 등)를 가리킵니다. 2020년 글은 라이브러리와 프레임워크를 React, Angular 편 과 Vue.js, Svelte, Stimulus 편 으로 나누었지만, 이번에는 한 글로 묶었습니다. 개별 프레임워크의 기능보다 프레임워크 사이에서 함께 일어난 변화(Signals로의 수렴, 서버로의 회귀, Rust 기반 빌드 도구로의 이동, 웹 표준의 흡수, AI 도구의 영향)가 더 크게 보였기 때문입니다. 2020년 글의 마지막 부분에서는 "어떤 프레임워크든 모두 JavaScript와 웹을 기반으로 하기 때문에 프레임워크 위주로 접근하기보다는 기본적인 기술을 깊게 이해하는 접근이 필요하다"라고 썼습니다. 이 글에서도 같은 관점을 유지합니다. 6년 동안 프레임워크들은 서로 다른 이름으로 같은 문제를 풀었고, 그 문제의 상당 부분은 결국 브라우저와 언어 표준 쪽으로 넘어가고 있습니다. 이번 연재는 다음 네 편으로 구성됩니다. 1편: JavaScript(ECMAScript) 2편: 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript 3편: WebAssembly 4편: 라이브러리와 프레임워크 이 글에서는 먼저 2020년 이후 React, Angular, Vue, Svelte, Preact의 변화를 정리합니다. 이어서 프레임워크 사이의 공통 흐름인 Signals와 메타 프레임워크, 프레임워크를 가리지 않는 도구 모음인 TanStack, 상태 관리, 빌드 도구, 테스트 도구, 웹 표준을 차례로 살펴봅니다. 마지막으로 AI 코딩 도구가 프레임워크 선택과 개발 방식에 가져온 변화를 정리합니다. 이 글의 내용은 2026년 10월을 기준으로 작성되었습니다. 글을 읽는 시점에 따라 글의 내용과 사실이 다를 수 있습니다. 2020년 이후 6년: 3(+1)대 프레임워크의 지금 2020년 글은 React, Angular, Vue를 3대 프레임워크로, Svelte를 '+1'로 놓았습니다. 당시 npm 다운로드 수로 보면 React는 Vue, Angular와 대략 4.5배 차이가 있었고, Svelte는 관심도에 비해 실제 도입은 아직 적었습니다. 6년 뒤의 숫자는 다음과 같습니다. 같은 주의 npm 주간 다운로드 수를 2020년 11월 첫 주와 2026년 10월 첫 주(9월 28일~10월 4일)로 비교했습니다. 표 1 npm 주간 다운로드 수 비교(출처: npm registry API , 패키지별 조회, 2026년 9월 28일~10월 4일) 패키지 2020년 11월 1일~7일 2026년 9월 28일~10월 4일 증가 react 8,869,607 224,422,510 약 25배 vue 1,962,540 20,397,470 약 10배 @angular/core 2,076,121 7,300,962 약 3.5배 svelte 101,464 7,724,778 약 76배 React와 Vue의 차이는 4.5배에서 약 11배로 벌어졌습니다. 다운로드 수에는 CI 환경의 반복 설치와 다른 패키지의 의존성으로 받는 경우가 섞여 있어 실사용자 수로 읽을 수는 없습니다. 다만 방향은 분명합니다. Svelte는 증가율이 가장 높아 이제 Angular와 비슷한 다운로드 수를 기록하고 있습니다. 설문 조사도 같은 경향을 보여 줍니다. State of JS 2025 (전체 응답자 13,002명)에서 '사용해 본 적 있다'의 비율은 다음과 같습니다. 표 2 State of JS 프런트엔드 프레임워크 사용률과 유지 의향(출처: State of JS 2025: Front-end Frameworks ) 프레임워크 2020 사용률 2025 사용률 2025 유지 의향(retention) React 80% 85% 72% Vue 48% 52% 84% Angular 55% 48% 48% Svelte 14% 27% 86% Preact 13% 15% 81% Solid - 10% 89% Lit 5% 10% 67% htmx - 9% 69% Alpine.js 3% 9% 77% 그림 1 State of JS 프런트엔드 프레임워크 사용률 추이(2016년~2025년)(출처: State of JS 2025: Front-end Frameworks ) 유지 의향은 '다시 사용하겠다'라고 답한 비율입니다. React는 사용률이 가장 높지만 유지 의향은 2020년 87%에서 2025년 72%로 내려왔고, 관심도(interest) 역시 58%에서 27%로 떨어졌습니다. 같은 조사에서 프런트엔드 프레임워크 사용 시 겪는 고충(주관식, 3,747명 응답) 1위는 '인지 부담(cognitive overload)'(1,066건), 2위는 '생태계 문제'(759건)였습니다. 특정 프레임워크의 문제보다 배우고 따라가야 할 것이 많다는 피로가 가장 큰 불만입니다. Solid는 사용률 10%에 불과하지만 5년 연속 유지 의향 1위를 기록했습니다. 그림 2 State of JS 프런트엔드 프레임워크 만족도(유지 의향) 추이(2016년~2025년)(출처: State of JS 2025: Front-end Frameworks ) 설문 주최 측은 2025년 결과를 "지난 1년간 사용률 순위에 변동이 없었다"라고 요약했습니다. Alpine.js와 htmx가 자리를 바꾼 것이 유일한 변화였습니다. 평균 응답자가 경력 전체에서 사용해 본 프레임워크 수는 2.6개였습니다. 매달 프레임워크를 갈아타는 개발자의 이미지는 사실과 거리가 있습니다(참고: State of JS 2025: Front-end Frameworks ). Stack Overflow 2026 개발자 설문 의 웹 프레임워크 항목(응답 10,281명)에서도 React가 41.5%로 Node.js(46.4%)에 이어 2위였고, Vue 17.2%, Angular 16.0%, Svelte 7.8% 순이었습니다. 2025년 조사 (React 44.7%, Angular 18.2%, Vue 17.6%)와 비교하면 Vue와 Angular의 순서가 바뀌었습니다. 그림 3 Stack Overflow 2026 개발자 설문의 웹 프레임워크와 웹 기술 사용 비율(출처: 2026 Stack Overflow Developer Survey: Technology ) 정리하면 2020년의 '3(+1)대' 구도는 'React와 나머지'로 바뀌었습니다. 다만 나머지가 정체한 것은 아닙니다. title: 2026년과 이후 JavaScript의 동향 - WebAssembly
abstract: 2020년 글 은 W3C 권고(1.0) 직후의 WebAssembly(이하 'wasm')를 다뤘습니다. '미래 버전에 포함될 작업'으로 스레드, SIMD(single instruction, multiple data), 참조 타입, 꼬리 호출, ESM(ECMAScript modules) 통합을 소개했고, Bytecode Alliance와 WASI(WebAssembly System Interface)가 그리는 브라우저 밖의 그림을 살펴봤습니다. 그리고 "아직까지 실서비스에서의 활발한 사용이 눈에 띄지는 않는다"라는 말과 함께, Sass가 wasm으로 플랫폼별 빌드 문제를 풀 수 있을지 모른다는 기대로 글을 맺었습니다. 이번 연재는 다음 네 편으로 구성됩니다. 1편: JavaScript(ECMAScript) 2편: 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript 3편: WebAssembly 4편: 라이브러리와 프레임워크 이 글에서는 2020년 글 이후 6년을 이어서 정리합니다. 2020년에 예고했던 기능들의 결말, wasm 2.0과 3.0, 지금 진행 중인 제안, WasmGC 덕분에 웹에서 쓸 수 있게 된 언어들, Component Model과 WASI가 바꾼 브라우저 밖의 생태계, JavaScript 개발자가 알게 모르게 쓰고 있는 wasm 패키지들을 살펴봅니다. 마지막으로 AI 도구와 에이전트가 wasm의 쓰임새를 어떻게 바꾸고 있는지도 정리합니다. 이 글의 내용은 2026년 10월을 기준으로 작성되었습니다. 글을 읽는 시점에 따라 글의 내용과 사실이 다를 수 있습니다. 2020년 이후 6년 2020년 글을 쓸 당시 wasm은 숫자 타입 네 가지( i32 , i64 , f32 , f64 )와 연속된 바이트 배열인 선형 메모리(linear memory)만 가진, 말 그대로 '컴파일 타깃'이었습니다. JavaScript와 문자열 하나를 주고받으려 해도 메모리에 바이트를 쓰고 그 위치를 숫자로 넘기는 글루 코드(glue code)가 필요했습니다. 6년이 지난 지금 wasm은 GC(가비지 컬렉션), 예외 처리, 64비트 주소 공간, 꼬리 호출을 명세에 담은 3.0이 되었습니다. Java, Kotlin, Dart 같은 GC 언어가 자체 런타임을 통째로 싣지 않고 wasm으로 컴파일됩니다. 브라우저 밖에서는 WASI가 Component Model 위로 옮겨 가며 0.2, 0.3이 나왔고, CDN 업체들이 wasm 기반 엣지 플랫폼을 운영하고 있습니다. 표 1 2019년 이후 주요 사건 시기 사건 2019년 12월 wasm 1.0 W3C 권고 2020년 10월 LibSass, Node Sass 비권장(deprecated) 지정 2023년 11월 V8 팀, WasmGC 포팅 가이드 공개(Chrome 119부터 WasmGC 지원) 2024년 1월 WASI 0.2 출시, WASI가 Component Model 기반으로 전환 2024년 6월 Google Sheets 계산 엔진의 WasmGC 전환 사례 공개 2024년 7월 Node Sass 지원 종료(end-of-life) 2024년 12월 W3C, wasm 2.0 후보 권고안 스냅샷 구현 요청 2025년 9월 wasm 3.0 발표 2025년 12월 Akamai, Fermyon 인수 발표 2026년 6월 WASI 0.3 출시, Safari 27 베타에서 JSPI(JS Promise Integration) 지원 Bytecode Alliance가 2026년 1월 발행한 10주년 회고 에 따르면, wasm은 2015년 6월 17일 4개 브라우저 벤더가 동시에 발표했고 2017년 말에 4대 브라우저가 모두 지원했습니다. 2019년 3월에 WASI가 발표되었고, 2024년 1월 WASI 0.2가 Component Model과 함께 나왔습니다. 2020년 '미래 버전에 포함될 작업'의 결말 2020년 글은 WebAssembly WG(Working Group)와 CG(Community Group)가 진행하던 작업으로 다섯 가지를 꼽았습니다. 6년이 지난 지금 다섯 항목 가운데 네 가지는 모든 주요 브라우저가 지원하지만, 명세상의 위치는 제각각입니다. 표 2 2020년에 소개한 기능의 현재 상태(2026년 10월 기준) 기능 명세상 위치 Chrome Firefox Safari 스레드 별도 제안(Phase 4) 74 79 14.1 128비트 SIMD wasm 2.0 91 89 16.4 참조 타입 wasm 2.0 96 79 15 꼬리 호출 wasm 3.0 112 121 18.2 ESM 통합 제안(Phase 3) 미지원 미지원 미지원 표 2의 브라우저 버전은 WebAssembly Feature Status 를, 제안의 단계는 WebAssembly/proposals 를 따랐습니다. 스레드 2020년 글은 Chrome 74부터 wasm 스레드가 기본 활성 상태라고 소개했습니다. 지금은 Firefox 79, Safari 14.1까지 지원 범위가 넓어졌습니다. 공유 메모리( SharedArrayBuffer )의 원자적 읽기와 쓰기, wait / notify 명령어로 구성된 이 제안 은 Phase 4(표준화 단계)에 있으며, 핵심 명세에는 아직 병합되지 않았습니다. 이 제안은 스레드 생성을 Web Workers에 맡기고, Emscripten 같은 툴체인이 이를 import로 노출하는 방식을 택했습니다. 공유 대상으로 정의한 것도 선형 메모리뿐이어서, 테이블, 전역 변수, WasmGC 객체는 스레드 사이에 공유할 수 없습니다. 이 한계를 다루는 후속 제안이 뒤에서 설명할 Shared-Everything Threads입니다. 128비트 SIMD 2020년 글에서 배열 4개 요소의 덧셈을 한 번의 CPU 명령으로 줄이는 예로 소개한 SIMD는 wasm 2.0에 Vector Instructions라는 이름으로 포함되었습니다. Chrome 91, Firefox 89, Safari 16.4부터 지원합니다(참고: Change History , WebAssembly Feature Status ). wasm 3.0에는 SIMD를 확장한 relaxed SIMD 가 추가되었습니다. 플랫폼별로 결과가 조금씩 다를 수 있는 연산(예: 융합 곱셈 덧셈)을 명세가 허용한 범위 안에서 하드웨어에 맞게 실행하도록 해 성능을 더 끌어냅니다. Chrome 114, Firefox 145에서 지원하고 Safari는 아직 플래그 뒤에 있습니다(참고: WebAssembly Feature Status ). 참조 타입 wasm 코드가 호스트 객체를 직접 참조하게 하는 참조 타입(reference types)은 wasm 2.0에 포함되었습니다. funcref 와 externref 두 가지 값 타입이 추가되었고, externref 로 JavaScript 객체를 wasm 쪽에서 숫자 인덱스로 바꾸지 않고 그대로 들고 있을 수 있게 되었습니다(참고: Change History ). 참조 타입은 이후 wasm 3.0의 typed function references와 GC의 바탕이 되었습니다. 꼬리 호출 추가 스택 공간을 쓰지 않고 함수를 호출하는 꼬리 호출(tail calls)은 wasm 3.0에 return_call , return_call_indirect 명령어로 포함되었습니다. 함수형 언어(Scheme, OCaml 등)의 컴파일러가 재귀를 반복문으로 바꾸는 우회 기법 없이 wasm을 생성할 수 있게 되었습니다(참고: Change History ). V8은 v11.2에서 꼬리 호출을 출시 했고, Emscripten으로 C++ 코루틴을 구현하는 사례를 함께 소개했습니다. 그림 1 꼬리 호출 시 호출자 프레임을 정리한 뒤 피호출 함수를 실행하는 스택 변화(출처: WebAssembly tail calls ) ESM 통합 다섯 항목 가운데 유일하게 아직 브라우저에 기본 탑재되지 않은 기능입니다. 제안은 Phase 3(구현 단계)에 있고, JavaScript 쪽 문법인 TC39의 Source Phase Imports도 Stage 3입니다(참고: WebAssembly/proposals , TC39 proposals ). 진행 상황은 뒤의 ' 진행 중인 제안 ' 절에서 자세히 설명합니다. wasm 2

title: NeurIPS Newsletter – October 2026

The NeurIPS Newsletter aims to provide an easy way to keep up to date with NeurIPS events and planning progress, respond to requests for feedback and participation, and find information about new initiatives. This newsletter will focus on NeurIPS 2026, held in Sydney, Australia, with […]

title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. To this end, we propose Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents. Coca-Cola compresses tool observations into latent tokens and embeds them into the input embedding space of the agent. We further introduce Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations. This trains the compression model to learn action-sufficient latent tokens that retain decision-critical information. Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces the agent's token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance. These results suggest that Coca-Cola offers a promising approach for context compression in agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/Coca-cola.

title: Signed but Steerable: Measuring and Closing the Text-Vector Integrity Gap in Offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Offline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices is updated through signed knowledge packs that carry text and precomputed embedding vectors. A signature proves who published a pack, not that its vectors encode its text. We study this text-vector integrity gap. A verifier that recomputes vectors and accepts them within a cosine tolerance concedes a predictable share of queries to an attacker who controls the vectors: the hijack rate equals the distribution of angular retrieval margins at the tolerance (the margin law). Margins are small in five corpora and two embedding models, so an idealised tolerance at the level of floating-point noise leaves up to 5.5% of queries exposed (at most 1.2% in any corpus once exact duplicate documents are excluded), and a threshold calibrated from our CPU INT8-FP32 comparison of a small embedding model (at the empirical 0.1% quantile of honest cosines) leaves 98-100% exposed; on a Raspberry Pi 5 running a local language model, such an attack lowers correct answers from 0.75 to 0.39. Integrity audits of compressed vector stores fare no better: on a FAISS product-quantisation index over 57,638 documents, tampered vectors that all pass the audit put the attacker's document first for 25% of targets. Verifying quantisation codes instead, with ambiguity decided by the verifier, a calibrated guard band and canonicalisation, accepted every honest vector in our samples on three platforms and left the publisher no choice. We also show that common floating-point and dynamic-INT8 inference pipelines are not bit-reproducible across batch sizes or architectures, and report pre-registered negative results on abstention, context pruning and semantic screening. We release code and data.

title: StepX-OPD: Rethinking Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Diffusion Models
abstract: A deployable text-to-image diffusion model must hold several capabilities at once, such as instruction following, text rendering and human preference, and must sample in a few steps. Capabilities and few-step sampling are built in separate stages: a full-step model first consolidates capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation, then serves as a fixed teacher for step distillation. Every full-step model we evaluate scores lower once compressed, and the second stage cannot begin until the first finishes. We introduce StepX-OPD, which merges the two stages: one student acquires every capability while learning to sample in a few steps, so frozen specialists supervise it on the states its own rollout visits rather than on a longer trajectory it never runs. Because a decomposition of the rollout's KL weights velocity mismatch most heavily near the clean end, we also regress the student's velocity on the low-noise part of the rollout. Separately, we find that capability integration makes models write prompt words into images on prompts that never asked for text, and we give a variant that lowers it. We evaluate on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev across instruction following, text rendering, image quality and human preference. On both architectures, StepX-OPD attains the highest normalized average score among the four-step methods compared and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD model, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD followed by step distillation.

title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.

title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling
abstract: Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended real-world problem into assumptions, a model, a solution, and a defended recommendation, and its answers matter only if they are both close to a credible reference and physically feasible; existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, leaving those numbers unchecked. We introduce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark to make complete contest-style modeling problems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once, over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems (2023--2025). Each task ships the verbatim statement, official attachments, and figures in a containerized terminal; the agent returns one JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of the final question against a reproduction of the Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scoring, which never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification---a programmatic gate over six decidable invariant forms plus 624 Lean~4 obligations---with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers rather than one, so a model must be close to many accepted answers; across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58\%, while the \2.54 open model holds 59.81% at 1/100$ the cost. TB-MathModel turns the numeric core of modeling into a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/terminal-bench-math-modeling.

title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

title: Information Games: Strategic Crowding and Firm Repositioning in Language-Model Space
abstract: When firms respond to new market opportunities, their capacity choices alter the future discounted free cash flows available to both competitors and investors. In competitive markets, these investment decisions publicized in news articles and analyst reports, measuring the changes in capital structure, product mix, firm leadership, risk exposure and operating procedure made by the firm. Modern search engines rely on Large Language Models to measure the relevancy of source documents to given search query. These measurements let researchers represent these news articles as clouds of dense vectors whose information geometry reflects the dissimilarity of firms over time. Building on Xu et al. (2022), we develop a model of costly competitive adjustment in which firms allocate capacity in which firms make firm capacity adjustment towards free cash flow shocks. Using a novel sandwich estimator, we analyse the sign and magnitude of this predicted adjustment using multi-agent simulation, and validate our findings on a sample of news and analyst reports from Nasdaq-listed companies between 2018-2022.

title: Reducing Representational Interference in Retrieval Embeddings with Trainable Prefix Tokens
abstract: Embedding models compress variable-length text into fixed-size vector representations, but this compression can entangle semantic content with residual token-level information, such as artifacts arising from attention sink behavior. We propose a simple method that prepends trainable [DUMP] tokens to the input during embedding model training. The method keeps the model architecture, pooling strategy, and training loss unchanged, while optimizing the added tokens through the standard contrastive retrieval objective. By introducing trainable prefix positions that interact with regular tokens during encoding, [DUMP] tokens help reduce the influence of residual or uninformative token-level signals on the final retrieval representation. Experiments on standard retrieval and long-context benchmarks show that our method consistently improves over finetuned baselines across encoder and decoder embedding models. Further analysis shows that [DUMP] tokens alter token-level activation and attention patterns associated with low-information tokens. These results suggest that trainable prefix tokens provide a lightweight way to improve retrieval representations.

title: Hard Sample-Conditioned Decorrelated Attention for Robust Face Recognition
abstract: Multi-head attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) allows independent attention patterns across heads, but without explicit regularization, heads may learn redundant patterns rather than complementary roles. Correlation-based penalties encourage head disentanglement, yet apply uniform regularization across all training samples. In face recognition (FR), hard samples whose embeddings lie close to competing identities are critical for optimization and generalization. Motivated by this, we propose ViT-HarDis, which conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty: samples with high cosine similarity to negative class centers receive stronger head decorrelation, enforcing specialization where identity ambiguity is highest. Experiments show improvements over both the baseline and uniform disentanglement on most benchmarks. Our analysis shows that ViT-HarDis reduces the similarity of hard samples to competing class centers while decreasing inter-head attention similarity, and that applying disentanglement only to the final transformer layers outperforms regularizing the entire network. Trained on WebFace4M, ViT-HarDis achieves SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank-1, while achieving the best IJB-B and TinyFace results when trained on MS1MV3, improving FR without architectural modifications or additional inference cost. Code: https://github.com/TaharChettaoui/Hard-Sample-Conditioned-Attention-for-FR.

title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer
abstract: Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-model Transfer (PACT), a form of latent communication between language models, combines a larger model's prompt representations with a smaller model's efficient generation, offering a promising way to balance capability and inference cost. However, existing systems provide limited support for independently evaluating large-small model collaboration, and improved task performance alone does not establish whether the receiver benefits from the sender's information. We introduce PLatour, an open-source PACT framework that connects frozen models through lightweight, zero-initialized linear bridges trained directly with task rewards and supports hybrid-attention architectures. PLatour significantly outperforms open-source baselines on generation tasks and surpasses Mostik's reported results on shared mathematics and coding benchmarks using a substantially smaller sender. However, controlled experiments show that the gains on some tasks can be reproduced by uninformative sender signals, self-communication, or receiver-only training. We find that trainable bridges can act as parameter-efficient adaptation mechanisms without exploiting useful sender information. We therefore propose PACT-Check to quantify how much of a trained PACT system's gain genuinely comes from communication. Finally, we discuss the opportunities and challenges of PACT systems. Code is available at https://github.com/zhenyi4/platour.

title: Towards Real-Time Full-Waveform LiDAR Transformers via Intensity-Guided Token Reduction and Physics-Aware Augmentation
abstract: LiDAR is a critical sensor for autonomous driving and robotics, yet it remains vulnerable to adverse conditions such as fog, rain, transparent objects, and low-reflectance surfaces. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL) addresses these limitations by capturing the complete return waveform as a histogram, preserving rich reflection characteristics including multi-path echoes and weak signals. While recent Transformer-based approaches have demonstrated promise on FWL data, two fundamental bottlenecks remain: high computational cost from redundant tokens in low-intensity background regions, and limited generalization due to scarce annotated training data. We address both bottlenecks by exploiting the physical structure inherent to FWL data. First, we propose FWL-ToPM, a token pruning and merging mechanism that leverages intensity distributions to selectively reduce tokens while retaining critical waveform content. Second, we introduce FWLAug, a data augmentation framework designed as a regularization method that preserves waveform structure, retaining the Time-of-Flight waveform of each ray and the frustum geometry, to improve generalization to unseen scenes. Evaluated on the Ghost-FWL benchmark, FWL-ToPM achieves over 8 times speedup at real-time throughput alongside a nearly 9-point F1 gain over the prior state of the art, establishing the first real-time FWL Transformer that simultaneously improves accuracy. FWLAug further improves performance on both the standard benchmark and an out-of-distribution test set of unseen scenes. Together, these methods push FWL-based perception toward practical deployment. The code and the OOD dataset are publicly available and can be accessed via the project page: https://keio-csg.github.io/FWL-ToPM

title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset
abstract: The pursuit of fair and equitable AI in human-centric tasks is critically hindered by the inherent biases and privacy risks of real-world datasets, which offer imbalanced representations of identity and often contain sensitive personal information. Consequently, state-of-the-art generative models trained on this skewed data exhibit unfair performance, particularly in identity-preserving generation. In this work we propose a pipeline for controllable generation of dataset with diverse faces for generative models training and finetuning. We achieve this by expanding foundational Arc2Face diffusion model with a flow matching generative model in the manifold of identity embeddings. We demonstrate that such approach achieves both goals of generative fidelity and label diversity not present in real human-centric datasets. As a result we collect and further contextualize a highly balanced identity-centric dataset of humans named SynthFaces. By design, our released images and identities are synthetic, reducing direct reliance on real personal images; we empirically check identity separation with a nearest-neighbor non-leakage metric. We purpose it for training and tuning of fair models for various downstream tasks, and showcase its usability in finetuning an existing adapter-based method for personalized generation.

title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
abstract: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

title: SAE Interprets MoE: Sparse AutoEncoders Reveal That MoE Experts Exhibit Human-Interpretable Fine-Grained Specialization
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a few of many experts, yet what an individual expert is responsible for remains unsettled. Existing analyses count how often an expert is selected on domain-labeled corpora, an instrument that fixes the taxonomy in advance, stays coarse, and records selection rather than contribution. We instead study specialization in feature space by training a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the output of an MoE layer. Since this output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs and the SAE encoder is affine, the pre-activation of every latent decomposes exactly over the experts. Aggregated over a corpus, this gives each expert a dominant set of latents whose activation it principally drives.
